text.p: ** BIRTHDAYS **
American revolutionary NATHAN HALE, who was hanged for spying on the British, was born in 1755.
Australian journalist DONALD MACDONALD, who became a sporting and war correspondent (the first at the Boer War), was born in 1859.

English explorer of the Antarctic, Captain ROBERT FALCON SCOTT, was born in 1868. Norwegian explorer ROALD AMUNDSEN beat him to the South Pole (placing a flag in the snow on the 14th of December, 1911), and SCOTT's body was discovered on the 10th of February, 1913.
German novelist THOMAS MANN, who wrote "Death In Venice", was born in 1875.
The first president of Indonesia AKHMED SUKARNO was born in 1901.
British philosopher SIR ISAIAH BERLIN was born in 1909.
Australian playwright ALAN SEYMOUR was born in 1927.
Australian Olympic swimmer JON HENDRICKS was born in 1935. He won two gold medals at the 1956 Melbourne Games (100-metre freestyle, 4x200-metre freestyle relay).

Exiled Tibetan leader, the DALAI LAMA, was born in 1935. He was chosen as the nation's spiritual leader on the 20th of July, 1939 and enthroned on the 22nd of February, 1940, going into exile in 1959.
Australian actor ANDREW MCFARLANE was born in 1951.

Swedish tennis player BJORN BORG was born in 1956. He won the men's singles title at Wimbledon 5 times, as well as 6 French Open titles, but has struggled since making a comeback to international tennis.
British singer and songwriter DEE C. LEE, who started her career singing backing vocals for 'Wham' and 'Style Council', was born in 1961. She went solo in 1985. Her hits include "See The Day" (1985).
** EVENTS **
1683 : The first public museum, The Ashmolean, was opened
at Oxford, England.
1891 : The first Prime Minister of Canada, SIR JOHN
ALEXANDER MACDONALD, died.
1908 : France paved the way with new divorce laws
granting automatic divorce after three years of legal separation.
1933 : The world's first drive-in movie theatre opened in
Camden, New Jersey, with accommodation for 500 cars.
1941 : Swiss-born American motor engineer LOUIS CHEVROLET
died.
1944 : Five desolate beaches on the Northern French

coast, (code-named UTAH, OMAHA, GOLD, JUNO and SWORD) became the scene of the largest military invasion in history. Under the supreme command of GENERAL DWIGHT D. EISENHOWER, an estimated one million men in 4,000 ships took part in the "D-DAY" landings known as 'Operation Overlord'. Planning for the invasion at Normandy began in January that year, and the final campaign to defeat Germany and its advancing forces had begun.
1949 : English author GEORGE ORWELL's novel "1984" was

published, in which he warned of "Big Brother" and the dangers awaiting society if politicians gained too much power. The book was seen as a development of his theme from "Animal Farm" (1945), which centered on the corrupting effects of political power.
1956 : American archeologist HIRAM BINGHAM, who
discovered the lost Inca city of Machu Picchu in Peru, died.
1957 : Britain handed Australia control of Christmas
Island, the island rich in phosphate north-west of Darwin.
1961 : Austrian psychoanalyst CARL GUSTAV JUNG, who once
said "Show me a sane man and I will cure him", died in Switzerland at the age of 85.
1976 : American oil billionaire JEAN PEAL GETTY, who'd
made his first million dollars at the age of 22, died in England, aged 83.
1980 : For the second time in a week, U.S. nuclear forces
went on red alert following a computer error warning of a Soviet attack.
1982 : American singers BOB DYLAN, STEVIE WONDER, JACKSON
BROWN and LINDA RONSTADT appeared at an anti-nuclear rally at the Rose Bowl in California.
1984 : Indian Prime Minister INDIRA GANDHI ordered the
storming of the Golden Temple in the Holy City of Amritsar, to arrest occupying Sikh militants. 712 Sikhs and 90 Indian soldiers died in the fighting.
1988 : DAVID STERN became the world's biggest
bubble-blower, blowing a bubble in New York measuring 15.24 metres in length.
1994 : Veterans of the D-Day landings at Normandy
commemorated the 50th anniversary of the Allied invasion.
1994 : A deadly, so-called "flesh-eating" bacteria that
surfaced in Britain was identified in the United States. The streptococcus bacteria was found in patients at a hospital in Connecticut.
1994 : A Chinese airliner on a domestic flight from the
tourist centre of Xian crashed killing all 160 people on board in the country's worst reported air accident.
1995 : Japanese Prime Minister TOMIICHI MURAYAMA and his
ruling coalition agreed to express "deep remorse" for Japan's acts of aggression in World War Two.
1996 : Britain and Ireland named former U.S. senator
GEORGE MITCHELL as chairman of all-party peace talks on Northern Ireland.
